Fabio, you have the first word. Why should anybody in this room be thinking about Brazil?
Let me set the scene with one number. Brazil adopted instant payments faster than almost any country in the world. Today most Brazilian adults pay each other in seconds.
That is a great sound bite. But cross-border is a different story, isn't it?

It is, and I'm glad you brought it up. Inside the country, a payment takes seconds. Across the border, the same company can wait two days and pay several times more in fees. That gap is the opportunity.
Let me push you a little. Some would argue that Brazil's regulation makes it too complex for global partners. How do you respond?
That's an important point, and I'd push back a little on it. The regulation is detailed, yes, but it is more predictable than most people think. For a partner, predictable is worth more than simple.
So what is your talking point for the partners in this room?
Start with one corridor. Brazil trades more with China than with any other country, and the United States is second. Those two corridors are where a partner learns the fastest.
We have thirty seconds left. A closing remark?
Brazil is not the easiest market in this room. It may be the one that grows the fastest, once the border stops being slower than the country.
Brazil is not the easiest market in this room, but it may be the fastest-growing.

When people present data, they almost always make the same mistake. They say the number, and then they rush to the next sentence as if they were embarrassed by it. The audience needs about one second to understand what a number means. So give them the number, stop, and count to one in your head. Then tell them what it means. Brazil adopted instant payments faster than almost any other country. Pause. That is the sentence people will repeat at dinner. The second mistake is comparing too many things at once. One comparison per sentence. Twice as fast, or half the cost, but not both in the same breath. And the third mistake is precision. Round your numbers. Nobody remembers forty-seven point three percent. Everybody remembers almost half.

When a speaker from an emerging market opens a panel, I am listening for three things, and I decide in about a minute. First, the size of the opportunity, in one number I can repeat. Not ten numbers. One. Second, the problem, stated honestly. If you tell me your market has no challenges, I stop believing everything else you say. If you tell me the regulation is complex but predictable, I start taking notes. And third, what it means for me. Most speakers explain their country beautifully and never say what a partner should actually do on Monday. The best Brazilian speaker I heard last year said: start with one corridor, we will give you the data, and in six months you will know. I called him the following week.

I have moderated maybe a hundred panels, so here is how it looks from my chair. Your opening statement is not the moment to say everything. It is the moment to give me one talking point I can come back to. If you give me five, I will pick the one you care about least. In the questions from the audience, the hard question is usually a gift. When somebody says your market is too risky, the room is not waiting for you to win the argument. They are waiting to see if you stay calm. Acknowledge it, answer it with one fact, and bring the conversation back to your talking point. And please, keep your closing remark under twenty seconds. The last sentence is the one they remember, so make it short enough to remember.
